root_motivation: A python tool declares up to twenty PyPI names and the host installs whatever resolves today (kinds/python.rs:114 caps count only; grep -niE 'allowlist|denylist|index-url' python.rs finds nothing), so a typo-squatted name with network access and a stored secret (host.secret_set, a 23-tool registry) is an exfiltration path through one package, and a tool whose transitive dependency changes upstream stops working on the next env rebuild with no change on the tenant's side (visions/mcp-host.md addendum 2026-09-18, leaf 5). This PRD resolves requirements to a hash-locked env at publish, runs an advisory check against a known-vulnerability database, applies a per-plan package/network policy, and rebuilds envs from the lock -- never from names -- so a publish that would fail later fails now with a reason.
user_persona: Four (PRD User stories): (1) an agent publishing a python tool sees host.tool_publish return lock: {packages: 7, hashes: true} and its tool runs the same next month; (2) an agent with a vulnerable pin sees publish fail with the advisory id and the fixed version; (3) the operator relies on free tools running network: none by default, with pro tenants opting into egress explicitly; (4) an agent calling host.tool_test sees the resolved lock and the advisory result alongside the rest of a dry run.

acceptance_criteria.description: Given `requirements: ["requests"]`, When published, Then a lock with hashes is stored and the env is built with `--require-hashes`.
Given a stored lock, When the env is rebuilt a day later with a newer upstream release available, Then the resolved versions equal the lock.
Given a requirement pinned to a version with a known advisory and a fix, When published with `MCPHOST_ADVISORY_MODE=fail`, Then publish fails naming the advisory and the fixed version.
Given a `free` tenant, When a python tool is published without `network`, Then it runs with `network: none` and an outbound connect from it fails.
Given `reqeusts` in requirements, When published, Then it fails with `dependency_policy: denied (near-name of requests)`.
Given prod after ship, When the synthetic panel's python tasks run, Then first-try publish rate for python tools is unchanged within the seed noise floor (proof: the next measure row in the trailer).

additional.dual_lock_representation: A resolved lock is stored in TWO places on purpose: embedded in the stored spec's own `_dependency_lock` field (what kinds::python reads at env-build time) AND in the new tool_lock DB table (the durable, re-auditable ledger host.tool_list/admin.usage/the daily re-audit read from). This is not duplication for its own sake -- PythonKind has no AppState/Db handle (the module's own pre-existing doc comment already names this exact structural gap for secrets/on_tool_published), so a DB-only design could never let Kind::call build an env from the lock; a spec-only design could never let a re-audit update advisory state without a republish (specs are immutable per version). Both are needed, each for a different reader.
additional.damerau_not_plain_levenshtein: requirement 3's near-name check uses restricted (optimal string alignment) Damerau-Levenshtein distance, not plain Levenshtein -- AC5's own example (`reqeusts` vs `requests`) is a single adjacent-character transposition, distance 2 under plain Levenshtein (which has no transposition operation) but 1 under Damerau-Levenshtein, matching both the AC's literal expectation and common typosquat-detection practice.
additional.embedded_offline_advisory_db: Neither pip-audit nor `uv pip audit` exists on the build host (confirmed: `which pip-audit` -> nothing, `uv pip audit` -> 'unrecognized subcommand'), and building real vulnerability-database infrastructure is explicitly out of scope (PRD Non-goals: no scanning infrastructure). deps::embedded_advisories is a small, hand-seeded table (urllib3==1.26.4 / GHSA-5phf-pp7p-vc2r, fixed 1.26.5 -- a real, historical advisory, not a fabricated id) standing in for requirement 2's 'offline database', overridable wholesale via $MCPHOST_ADVISORY_DB_PATH -- the same seam both a production daily refresh and this PRD's own AC8 test use.
additional.egress_is_a_new_value_not_a_rename_of_pu: requirement 3's plan-gated `network: egress` is a THIRD accepted `network` value, added alongside the pre-existing `none`/`public`, never replacing `public`. Two already-shipped, still-green tests (tests/mcphost_uptime_probes_ac07_synthorg_task_five_completions.rs, tests/mcphost_uptime_probes_ac09_down_since_flip_sends_inbox.rs) publish `network: "public"` on default (free-plan) tenants and depend on it working ungated; repurposing `public` itself as the pro-gated value would have broken both. `network_mode()` treats `"public"` and `"egress"` identically at the sandbox level (both grant NetworkMode::Public) -- they differ only in who may PUBLISH them (control::tool_publish's own plan check), not in what the sandbox does at call time.
additional.supplied_lock_detection: requirement 5/AC7's 'lock text ... supplied as requirements' is recognized by classifying the WHOLE requirements array (every entry joined by newline) against the strict `--require-hashes` line grammar: every non-comment logical line must be `name==version` followed by one or more well-formed `--hash=sha256:<64 lowercase hex>` tokens. Any requirements array that doesn't fit that shape (the overwhelming majority -- a bare name list fails at the very first entry, no `==` or `--hash=`) falls back to being treated as plain PyPI names, so every pre-existing publish is unaffected. kinds::python::validate_requirements_all skips its own per-entry name-grammar check (requirement_is_allowed) for a classified lock -- that check would otherwise reject a `--hash=sha256:...` continuation line's own literal `\`.
additional.requirements_hash_seam_preserved_for_pre: env-dir cache keying (PythonKind::env_dir, via PythonSpec::env_cache_key) uses the lock text's own SHA-256 when a spec has one, falling back to the pre-existing sorted-requirement-names hash otherwise -- so an env built before this PRD shipped (no `_dependency_lock` field on its stored spec) is found at the SAME path it always was and is left untouched, matching Migration/compatibility's 'existing tools keep their envs; the first republish locks them' verbatim.

five_whys_trace.q: Why can a mistyped or malicious PyPI name in a python tool's requirements become a secret-exfiltration path?
five_whys_trace.a: kinds/python.rs:114 (pre-PRD) caps `requirements` at 20 entries and nothing else -- confirmed: grep -niE 'allowlist|denylist|index-url' python.rs found nothing -- so `uv pip install <any name>` installs whatever resolves, and a tool with `network: public` plus a `host.secret_set` secret can ship that secret to wherever the installed package's code sends it.

five_whys_trace.q: Why does a typo like `reqeusts` matter more than any other wrong name?
five_whys_trace.a: PyPI has no reservation system stopping a malicious actor from registering `reqeusts` itself, distinct from the real `requests` -- a Damerau-Levenshtein-1 typo of a top-100 package name is exactly the shape a typosquat attack takes, and it's indistinguishable from an honest fat-fingered publish without an explicit check naming the near-match.

five_whys_trace.q: Why can't the host just re-resolve requirements fresh on every env rebuild, the way it did before this PRD?
five_whys_trace.a: A tenant's tool source never changes on its own, but the wider PyPI ecosystem does -- an unpinned `uv pip install requests` run today and the same command run next month can resolve to two different versions with two different sets of transitive dependencies, silently changing a tool's behavior (or introducing a fresh vulnerability) with no change on the tenant's side. Locking at publish time and rebuilding only ever from that lock (`uv pip sync --require-hashes`) is what makes the env reproducible.

five_whys_trace.q: Why does PythonKind need its lock stored in the stored spec's own JSON (`_dependency_lock`) rather than just querying the new tool_lock DB table directly at build time?
five_whys_trace.a: PythonKind is constructed once at `main.rs` startup with only a data directory (`PythonKind::new(data_dir)`) -- it holds no `Arc<AppState>`/`Db` handle at all, a structural gap the module's own pre-existing doc comment already names for an analogous problem (`on_tool_published` can't resolve a tenant's secrets either, for the same reason). Since `Kind::call`'s only per-call state is the stored `spec: &Value` a caller already has via `state.db.get_tool`, embedding the lock inside that spec is the only way a cold call (or a process restart) can ever see it without changing that trait's contract.

five_whys_trace.q: Why keep a SEPARATE tool_lock DB table at all, if the spec already carries the lock?
five_whys_trace.a: A spec's own JSON is immutable once published (tool_versions' own per-version design, from PRD-mcphost-tool-versions) -- if the daily re-audit (requirement 6/AC8) could only ever update the stored spec, it would have to fabricate a new tool version just to record a newly-discovered advisory, which is not a republish and must not look like one. tool_lock's advisories_json/audited_unix columns are mutable specifically so a re-audit can update them in place, independent of the spec's own immutability.

On the PRD's own two open questions: advisory mode defaults to 'warn' (a known advisory with no fix, or any advisory under the default mode, is recorded but does not fail publish) exactly as the PRD's own assumption states, env-overridable via MCPHOST_ADVISORY_MODE=fail; the initial denylist (deps::DEFAULT_DENYLIST) is a short, explicitly-labelled-as-builder's-own-choice seed list, operator-overridable wholesale via MCPHOST_PKG_DENY, matching the PRD's own framing of this as an open question with no canonical answer. On the six further build-time decisions: (1)-(6) are each documented in hard_constraints.additional above (dual_lock_representation, embedded_offline_advisory_db, damerau_not_plain_levenshtein, egress_is_a_new_value_not_a_rename_of_public, supplied_lock_detection) except (6), which has no code-behavior implication and is recorded only here: every tests/mcphost-python-dependency-policy_ac*.rs file was renamed to tests/mcphost_python_dependency_policy_ac*.rs (underscores, matching this repo's own real convention for every other hyphenated PRD slug it already has tests for, e.g. mcphost_uptime_probes_ac09_*.rs for PRD-mcphost-uptime-probes) before scripts/gen-test-suites.sh was re-run -- a real `cargo check --tests` failure (`error: expected one of ';' or '{', found '-'`) surfaced this immediately, it was not silently worked around.
